title: A novel Bayesian approach to reconnecting families through DNA
question: Distant relatives can be difficult to distinguish from unrelated individuals using limited genetic evidence. I developed a workflow that simulates competing relationship hypotheses and estimates their support, then evaluated it across eleven pedigrees using repeated cross-validation and shuffled-label checks.
method: Developed an Approximate Bayesian Computation pipeline that simulates DNA-sharing patterns under competing pedigree hypotheses, summarizes shared segments and estimates support for related versus unrelated models. The capstone examines 11 pedigrees and includes repeated cross-validation and label-permutation checks.
finding: The framework makes the relationship hypothesis, reference populations and uncertainty explicit. It was motivated by humanitarian identification work in Argentina, where ambiguous genetic evidence has consequences for families.
limit: Internal cross-validation measures performance within the constructed reference banks. It is not a real-world identification accuracy estimate, and should not be directly compared with STR detection power as though the metrics were interchangeable.
label: pedigrees examined
role: Capstone research · Institute of Calculus, University of Buenos Aires

title: Vinyl beyond release week
question: National sales showed vinyl growing while CDs declined. Did individual albums tell the same story? I constructed a dataset from scattered public sales reports, compared formats at launch and later dates, and investigated the older recordings behind the market totals.
method: Combined RIAA market trends, publicly reported album sales and industry catalog breakdowns.
finding: Older recordings account for a larger share of vinyl purchases than CD purchases.
label: albums in the opening-week dataset

title: Huzur: a Mongolian card game platform
question: Can an AI opponent play a traditional Mongolian card game better than I do? I’ve been playing since I was six! I built this platform to keep playing with friends after graduation took us to different countries.
method: Built a browser game for 2–5 players, with local human and AI seats, multiplayer lobbies and persistent match records. AI decisions combine strategic heuristics, lookahead and exact two-player endgame search. Offline self-play supports policy comparisons.
finding: The project connects a playable product with an evaluation loop: log decisions, simulate opponents, compare policies and revise the strategy. Fairness guards keep hidden opponent cards and deck order out of bot decision inputs.
limit: Simulated match results do not establish performance against human players. The documented multiplayer roadmap still includes server-side rules validation.
label: players supported

title: Same trainees. Different controls. Opposite conclusions.
question: Can observational methods recover an experimental result? I tested matching methods against a randomized job-training benchmark, then explored synthetic control in a separate application.
method: Analyzed job-training outcomes using experimental and observational data, propensity-score and genetic matching, and instrumental variables. A second application uses synthetic control and placebo diagnostics to examine California’s 2011–2015 drought and crime.
finding: The job-training exercise illustrates why treatment selection matters: a naive observational comparison can reverse the direction of the randomized comparison. Matching is assessed against the experimental benchmark; the drought analysis makes the counterfactual and placebo evidence explicit.
limit: These are course analyses, not new randomized experiments. Causal interpretations depend on balance, identification assumptions and the credibility of the comparison group.

title: What makes an expensive home an outlier?
question: I compared three Bayesian models of Buenos Aires property prices to investigate how assumptions about unusual observations change the results.
method: Compared Normal, Student-t and outlier-aware Bayesian regression specifications for Buenos Aires property pricing.
finding: Treating the likelihood as a modeling decision makes the influence of unusual observations visible. The report compares specifications rather than relying on a single error model.
limit: Results describe the project dataset and modeling assumptions; they are not a deployed appraisal system.

title: I simulated the male loneliness epidemic
question: Isolation, algorithmic exposure, and weakening friendships can reinforce each other. I built an agent-based simulation to explore that feedback loop, then compared interventions targeting the algorithm, social support, and friendship influence.
method: Built an agent-based Monte Carlo simulation on weighted friendship networks. Isolation, exposure, ideological drift and friendship decay interact; intervention scenarios change amplification and social support.
finding: The model provides a way to explore feedback loops and compare interventions under a common set of assumptions. Network dynamics reveal behavior that a static average would hide.
limit: These are simulated outcomes. The model does not establish empirical causal effects of recommendation systems or real interventions.

title: No individual scores. Different bins. Still comparable?
question: All I had were score ranges and counts, and even the ranges changed between years! I built Bayesian models that worked directly with each histogram’s bin boundaries, allowing me to compare underlying score distributions without pretending I had individual records. The project uses synthetic data inspired by inconsistent reporting of test scores.
method: Modeled latent test-score distributions from grouped observations, comparing pooling choices across years while retaining the information represented by each histogram bin.
finding: The analysis tackles a common practical problem: the raw records are unavailable, yet a comparison is still needed. Probabilistic modeling expresses uncertainty instead of pretending the bin midpoints are individual observations.
limit: The conclusions depend on distributional assumptions and the information retained in the published histograms.

title: I turned my IMDb ratings into a machine-learning experiment
question: Using 615 ratings I’d collected over the years, I explored what genres, plots, and posters reveal about my movie preferences. Can a model figure out my taste?
method: Aligned 568 titles from 615 collected IMDb ratings. Compared 36 metadata features with ResNet-50 poster embeddings and TF-IDF/SVD text representations using dimensionality reduction, classification and modality ablations.
finding: The exploratory run suggested that adding high-dimensional poster and text features did not automatically improve on metadata. The public notebook replaces the primary comparison with fold-local preprocessing pipelines.
limit: The original evaluation fitted preprocessing before the train/test split. A leakage-free rerun is still needed; historical performance estimates are not presented as validated generalization results.
label: aligned movie titles

title: Forum: AI notes and a database for Minerva classes
question: A team-built platform that turns class recordings into searchable transcripts and notes. My contribution focused on the relational database and data-integrity testing.
method: Worked on a team-built course platform that connects recording uploads, FFmpeg audio extraction, Whisper transcription and AI-generated summaries, topics and action items. The application uses Flask, React and SQLite, with course membership controlling access.
finding: The platform brings recordings, transcripts and notes into one searchable workflow. My contribution focused on the relational database and data-integrity testing. The project includes session-processing states and preserves transcripts when note generation fails.
limit: Team course project, not a claim of sole authorship. The public repository documents the implementation and setup; the linked video demonstrates the application.

title: Wrigley: the price of leverage
question: A $3 billion debt-funded payout looks attractive when you count the tax shield. What happens when you count financial distress too? I combined valuation scenarios with interest-coverage constraints to assess how much debt the company could reasonably take on.
method: Compared tax-shield value, post-recapitalization borrowing costs, interest coverage and expected distress costs. Examined dividends versus repurchases and the difference between EPS mechanics and shareholder value.
finding: The report’s no-distress tax shield is $1.2 billion. Its B-rated base scenario reduces net value creation to $732 million; a higher conditional distress loss reduces it to $576 million. The recommendation is sensitive to the debt capacity and distress assumptions.
limit: The linked report is labeled a working draft. Values are case-model estimates, not realized outcomes; the distress scenarios depend on assumed conditional losses.

title: An AI boom is easier to forecast than to value
question: Our team valued CoreWeave using discounted cash flow, public comparables, and precedent transactions. The methods disagreed substantially. Why?
method: The team combined a DCF, public comparables and precedent transactions, with sensitivity analysis around financing costs, terminal growth, investment and working capital.
finding: The April 2025 report presents a $10-per-share base DCF estimate and a $22 synthesis across methods. The important analytical issue is the spread between methods and the sensitivity to long-run assumptions.
limit: This is a dated team case analysis, not a current price target. Segment-based comparables and terminal-value assumptions require particular care.
role: Team course project · Undral Ganbaatar, Shazil Farukh & Anne Behme

title: Toyota: financial policy across borders
question: How do production location, currency exposure, and financial subsidiaries change the way we interpret an automaker’s balance sheet?
method: Compared Toyota’s financial ratios with automaker peers, then examined domestic production, international competitiveness and financial policy in the case’s 2010–2011 setting.
finding: The case connects balance-sheet decisions to operating geography. A consolidated ratio alone can obscure the different funding needs of manufacturing and financial services.
limit: Historical peer comparisons depend on consistent segment definitions. The case is not a statement about Toyota’s current financial position.

title: Two investments look profitable. What has to go right?
question: For Aditya Birla’s proposed international investments, project profits were only part of the story. I adjusted cash flows for ownership and remittances to value what the parent company would receive, then examined how much depended on terminal value.
method: Developed an India–UAE SME payments and working-capital proposal and an UltraTech investment proposal. Built parent-level cash-flow forecasts, ownership adjustments and valuation scenarios.
finding: The base models produce positive parent NPVs for both proposals. Their attractiveness depends on execution, volume, terminal value and the group’s ability to apply existing capabilities.
limit: These are proposed investments and assumption-based forecasts, not projects implemented by the company.

title: A profitable investment. An uncomfortable financing problem.
question: Astral Records’ equipment investment had a small positive modeled NPV and a much larger funding requirement. I examined whether the company could finance the decision.
method: Reviewed historical profitability and leverage, then forecast 1994–1995 financial statements with and without capital expenditure. Connected operating performance to financing requirements.
finding: Revenue growth alone does not answer the funding question. The case brings margin pressure, debt servicing and capital spending into the same forecast.
limit: Historical classroom case; projections depend on the case inputs and operating assumptions.

title: Sales up. Profits up. Where’s the cash?
question: Science Technology planned rapid growth while improving efficiency. I connected its income forecast to receivables, inventory, and financing needs, showing why a shorter cash cycle could still leave the company needing substantially more working capital.
method: Examined a plan that accelerates sales growth beyond the historical rate. Reconstructed the cash conversion cycle, working-capital needs and reliance on short-term borrowing.
finding: The forecast illustrates how rising accounting income can coexist with cash pressure. Inventory and receivables become central to the credibility of the growth plan.
limit: Forecast improvements in inventory management are assumptions, not observed achievements.

title: Raise another million. How much of the company is left?
question: I used a venture valuation model to compare how two funding amounts change the ownership bargain for RVD.AI.
method: Built a market-sizing and revenue scenario, applied a venture-capital valuation method and compared $2.5 million and $3.5 million funding cases. Examined sensitivity to market share and required returns.
finding: In the report’s fixed post-money valuation scenario, larger funding sharply increases the investor’s ownership requirement. The case makes the growth-versus-dilution tradeoff explicit.
limit: Market share, exit multiples and future margins are scenario assumptions. This is a historical academic analysis, not a completed financing.

title: Same exit. Different fine print. Millions apart.
question: Two financing structures can divide the same exit proceeds very differently. I modeled Optiguard’s capitalization and payout waterfalls to quantify how liquidation preferences and antidilution terms change what investors and founders receive.
method: Modeled ownership and option reserves, a hypothetical Series B, antidilution adjustments and conventional versus participating liquidation preferences.
finding: Valuation is only one part of the bargain. Exit payouts, dilution and control provisions change the economics for founders and investors.
limit: Hypothetical case scenarios; the analysis does not describe an executed investment.

title: Before opening another ice cream shop, follow the cash
question: A Freddo expansion analysis connecting marketing, inventory, payment terms, and working-capital requirements.
method: Examined receivables, inventory and payables, then developed operational and expansion scenarios including local production and changes in payment terms.
finding: The proposal connects expansion with cash discipline: faster collections and shorter inventory cycles can matter as much as new locations.
limit: Shipping costs, target cash-cycle days and expansion benefits are estimates. They are not verified cost savings or realized outcomes.

title: Can predators be too successful?
question: I built a spatial bunny–fox ecosystem, then varied reproduction and movement to explore when predators coexist with their prey and when the system collapses. Comparing local patterns with mean-field theory reveals what population averages can miss.
method: Simulated local population densities on a toroidal grid, conducted parameter sweeps, and compared stationary balances with theory.
finding: Spatial structure and model parameters change coexistence and collapse outcomes.
limit: Synthetic density model; ecological conclusions are conditional on its rules.

title: More security lanes. Same bottleneck?
question: Airport queues do not behave like independent service stations when they share a senior screening officer. I implemented a discrete-event simulation and compared it with queueing approximations to examine the hidden bottleneck.
method: Modeled shortest-queue routing, shared secondary screening, and repeated simulation runs.
finding: The report compares congestion and utilization across station counts.
limit: Scenario results, not measured airport outcomes; no staffing cost optimization.
role: Team CS166 course project · Undral and Navneet
